summary: Mid-debug: root cause found, fix half-applied, one open question, one deferred side-bug.

facts.fact: Goal: fix the intermittent CI failure of test_due_date_rollover.
Root cause: code compares a UTC date against date.today() (local time); the CI runner is on Pacific time, so between ~23:40 and midnight UTC the dates differ by one day.
DST was considered and ruled out.
Monkeypatching time.time was tried and does not work, because the C implementation of date.today() doesn't go through time.time. That edit was reverted.
User constraint: no new dev dependencies (pytest only), so freezegun is rejected; inject a clock instead.
Done (uncommitted): due.py now takes a clock parameter (defaulting to UTC now) on compute_due_date and days_until_due, and normalizes issued_at to UTC.
Still to do: schedule.py overdue() (line ~20) uses naive datetime.now().date() and must take and use a clock.
Still to do: rewrite test_due_date_rollover to use a fixed clock at 23:50 UTC, so it's deterministic without faketime.
Repro/acceptance command: TZ=America/Los_Angeles faketime '2026-09-27 16:50:00' uv run pytest tests/test_due.py (or equivalent), which must pass.
Open question, blocked on the user (who is asking the billing team): are stored issued_at values naive or timezone-aware? Don't guess.
Deferred, not now: money.format_currency uses ROUND_HALF_EVEN, the likely cause of the one-cent 'penny bug'.

traps.trap: Proposes adding freezegun or any new dev dependency.
Proposes monkeypatching time.time as the fix.
Plans to work on the format_currency rounding as part of the next step.
Asserts an answer to whether stored issued_at is naive or aware, or proceeds as if it's settled.
